en: The *Yujie jing* (Sūtra of the Noble Lady), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Tanwulan of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha...
He was preaching the Dharma for the fourfold assembly of disciples.

At that time, at the home of Anāthapiṇḍada, his son had previously married a daughter from an eminent family; her name was Yashodharā. She was beautiful and lovely, yet she gave rise to arrogance and did not serve her mother-in-law or father-in-law with the proper etiquette of a wife.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his wife deliberated together, saying:

"Our daughter-in-law is disobedient and does not follow the rules of propriety. If we apply corporal punishment, she will refuse to carry out these tasks; yet if we leave her uncorrected, her faults will only increase further. What should we do?"

The elder said, "Only the Buddha, the Great Sage, is well able to transform sentient beings; he can subdue even the most stubborn and fierce so that none dare not comply. I pray that you invite the Buddha to come and transform us.
His wife said:
"Excellent! At dawn, she dressed in her finest attire and went to the Buddha's dwelling. Prostrating herself with her head to the ground, she addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In my household, I have taken a wife for my son who is exceedingly arrogant; she does not serve my son with proper decorum. I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to visit our home tomorrow with his disciples for a meal, and that you will preach the Dharma to Yujia, so that her mind may be opened and she may reform her ways to practice virtue."
The Buddha said to the householder:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, he rejoiced, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed. Returning home, he observed the fast and prepared the midday meal.

On the following day, the Buddha arrived at the householder’s residence with one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples. The householder welcomed the Buddha with joy and paid him homage. Once the Buddha and the assembly were seated, everyone—both great and small—came forth to bow to the Buddha and withdrew to stand aside; however, Yama fled and hid herself, refusing to pay homage to the Buddha.

The Buddha immediately performed a transformation, causing the house, walls, and buildings of the elder’s residence to become like the color of lapis lazuli and crystal, so that the interior and exterior could see one another. When Yaya saw the Buddha with his thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his body the color of purple-gold and his radiance shimmering brilliantly, she was struck with awe and fear; her heart leaped and her hair stood on end. She immediately came forth to prostrate before the Buddha, bowing her head to repent, and then withdrew to stand on his right side.
The Buddha told Yuye:
"A woman ought not to rely on her own physical beauty to treat her husband with contempt.
What is meant by 'physical beauty'?"

To eliminate eighty-four perverse dispositions and to fix the mind with single-minded concentration is what constitutes true rectitude; it is not by means of complexion, facial features, or the color of one's hair that one is considered upright.
Within the female body there are ten evils. What are these ten?
First, when a woman is first born and falls to the ground, her parents do not rejoice.
Second, in raising and nurturing her, they find no joy.
Third, the minds of women are constantly fearful of others.
Fourth, their parents perpetually worry about their marriage.
Fifth, they are separated from their parents during their lifetime.
Sixth, she is constantly fearful of her husband’s gaze; she rejoices whenever he is pleased, yet trembles with dread whenever he is angry.
Seventh, she experiences great difficulty in conceiving and giving birth.
Eighth, in their youth, women are constrained by their parents;
ninth, in middle age, they are controlled by their husbands;
tenth, in old age, they are rebuked by their children and grandchildren—from birth until death, they never attain independence.
"These are the ten matters that women do not realize for themselves.
Yuye knelt with her hands joined in reverence and said to the Buddha:
"Having received this lowly body, I am unacquainted with the rules of propriety."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will fully explain the teachings and instructions regarding the duties of a wife.
The Buddha told Yuye:
“In serving her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband, there are five virtues and three evils.”
What are the five virtues?

First, as a wife, one should go to bed late and rise early; one should comb and adorn the hair, adjust the clothing, wash and wipe the face so that no filth remains, attend to tasks only after first informing those who are honored, always maintain a mind of respect and obedience, and even if there is something sweet and delicious, one must not eat it before [the husband].
Second, when her husband scolds or reviles her, she must not harbor anger or resentment.
Third, she must single-mindedly attend to her husband and must not think of illicit lust.
Fourth, she should always wish for her husband’s long life; whenever he goes abroad, the wife shall properly organize the household.
Fifth, one should always mind the husband’s goodness and not mind his faults;
these are the five virtues. What are the three evils?

First, failing to serve one’s mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband with the decorum of a wife; instead, desiring fine food, one eats it first; one goes to bed early before nightfall and does not rise when the sun comes up; when the husband wishes to instruct or reprimand her, she glares at him with angry eyes, responding with defiance and even cursing him.
Second, she does not direct her mind single-mindedly toward her husband, but instead thinks only of other men.
Third, she desires that her husband die so that she may remarry early; these are the three evils.
Yuye remained silent and had no words with which to answer the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Yuye:
"In this world, there are seven kinds of wives: [text continues]"

First, a wife like a mother; second, a wife like a younger sister; third, a wife like a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); fourth, a wife like a wife; fifth, a wife like a servant; sixth, a wife like an enemy; seventh, a wife like a life-taker. These are the seven types of wives; do you understand them?
Yujia addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not know what these seven wives have done;
I pray that the Buddha will explain it for me."
The Buddha told Yuye:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon this well. I shall analyze and explain it for you.
What constitutes a mother-wife?"

A mother-wife is one who loves her husband as dearly as a compassionate mother; she attends to him morning and night, never departing from his side, and serves him with all her heart, never missing the proper occasion. When her husband goes out or returns, she fears others might treat him with contempt; upon seeing him, she regards him with affection and tireless devotion, cherishing her husband as if he were her own son—this is what constitutes a mother-wife.
What is meant by a "sister-wife"?

A sister-wife is one who serves her husband with the utmost sincerity and respect, regarding him as if he were a brother—sharing the same vital breath yet divided in form—a close relative of bone and flesh with whom there is no duplicity of heart; she honors and reveres him just as a younger sister serves an elder brother. This is what is meant by a sister-wife.
What is meant by a wife who is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?

She serves her husband with sincere and profound affection, clinging to him with such devotion that she cannot bear to be parted from him. She constantly informs him of private matters; when he commits a fault, she reproaches him accordingly so that his conduct remains without error. She honors him in virtuous deeds, causing his wisdom to increase and become ever more clear. Out of mutual love, she desires to lead him across the world [to liberation] just as a spiritual friend does; this is what is meant by a wife who is a spiritual friend.
What constitutes a "womanly woman"? She honors great beings with sincerity and the utmost respect;

she serves her husband with humility and obedience to his commands. Rising early and retiring late, she reverently attends to his words and instructions. Her mouth utters no idle speech, and her body commits no idle act. She yields credit for virtues to others while taking blame upon herself for faults. She instructs with benevolence and generosity, exhorting him toward the Way. Her mind is upright and single-minded, free from any trace of depravity. She diligently cultivates the virtues of a wife, never failing or neglecting them. Advancing, she does not violate propriety; retreating, she does not lose decorum. She prizes harmony above all—this is what it means to be a "womanly woman."
What is meant by a "slave-wife"?
She always maintains a sense of fear and caution, not daring to be arrogant; she attends to her tasks with earnest diligence, having no aversion or hesitation;

her mind is always respectful and reverent, exhausting herself in loyalty and filial piety; her speech is gentle, her nature is always harmonious and conciliatory, and her mouth never commits the offense of harshness.
She does not harbor evil speech, nor does her body engage in the conduct of negligence. She is upright, sincere, pure, simple, honest, and trustworthy;
she is always self-disciplined and conducts herself with propriety. When her husband shows her favor, she is not arrogant;
even if he does not receive her, she does not feel resentment. Should she be struck with a staff, she accepts her share of it without anger. Furthermore, when she sees...
When reviled, she remained silent and harbored no resentment; she accepted it with a willing heart and joy, never entertaining a second thought.

She encouraged her husband in his virtues and did not envy his voice or beauty. When treated with partiality or meanness, she did not petition for justice. She was intent on cultivating the virtues of a wife, making no distinction between fine or coarse food and clothing.
She was single-mindedly diligent and reverent, fearing only that she might fall short, as she respectfully served her husband and attended to the household like a maidservant.
This is what is meant by a "slave-wife. What is meant by a "hostile wife"? She sees her husband with displeasure and constantly harbors anger;

day and night she thinks only of how to separate from him. Lacking the heart of a wife, she is always like a guest; she barks and quarrels without any sense of awe or restraint. Her hair is disheveled and she sleeps in a slouch, unfit for any task. She does not care to manage the household or support her children; she may even engage in lewdness without shame. Her appearance is like that of a dog or a beast, bringing disgrace upon her kin. Like an enemy, such is the hostile wife. This is what is meant by a hostile wife.
What is meant by a "life-taking wife"?
Day and night she does not sleep, harboring a heart of resentment as she faces her husband. She constantly thinks, "By what means can I separate from him?

Desiring to give him poison, she fears he might discover it; thus she sends it to relatives, whether near or far. Thus, with constant malice, she seeks to harm him. Whether she uses precious objects to hire someone to kill him, or employs a paramour to lie in wait and slay him—thus taking her husband's life through resentment and injustice—this is called a life-taking wife.
"These are the seven kinds of wives.
Yuye remained silent.
The Buddha said to Yuye:

"The five kinds of virtuous wives always possess a distinguished reputation; their words and deeds are governed by the Dharma, and they are loved and respected by all. Their kinsmen and the nine branches of their clan alike enjoy their prosperity. Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits all come to protect them so that they do not suffer injustice or calamity. After a hundred thousand lifetimes, they shall be reborn in celestial palaces of the seven treasures, where attendants naturally serve them on all sides. Their lifespan shall be extended, and they may indulge their every desire in unspeakable happiness."
When their lifespan in heaven is exhausted, they descend to be born in the human world as the descendants of wealthy and noble lords or princes;

they will be handsome, intelligent, and honored by all. As for that wicked wife, she shall constantly suffer an evil reputation, causing her present body to find no peace; she will frequently be afflicted by malevolent spirits and various poisons, remaining restless whether lying down or rising, and being terrified by nightmares. Her wishes shall not be fulfilled, and she shall encounter many calamities and misfortunes. After ten thousand lifetimes, when her soul receives a new form, she shall enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, wandering through these three miserable paths for countless kalpas without end.
The Buddha said to Yuye,
"Of these seven kinds of wives, which one do you wish to become?
Yuye shed tears and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:

"What my mind has done was born of folly and a lack of wisdom. From this day forward, I shall reform my past and cultivate my future; I shall serve my mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband like a maidservant, and for as long as I live, I shall never again dare to be arrogant."
The Buddha said to Yuyé:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Who among men is without fault?
He who is able to reform is as virtuous as one could be.
Yuye then stepped forward and requested to receive the ten precepts to become an upāsikā.
The Buddha told Yuye: "The first precept is that one must not kill living beings;

the second, that one must not steal or take the property of others; the third, that one must not commit adultery with other men; the fourth, that one must not drink alcohol; the fifth, that one must not speak falsely; the sixth, that one must not use harsh abuse; the seventh, that one must not engage in frivolous speech; the eighth, that one must not be jealous; the ninth, that one must not harbor anger; and the tenth, that one should believe that performing good deeds brings merit while committing evil deeds incurs retribution."

"Faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus—these constitute the ten precepts for an upāsikā, which one shall practice throughout one's life and not dare to transgress.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the disciples prostrated themselves in homage.
The Elder Anāthapiṇḍada, his wife, his children, and his daughter-in-law all offered water for washing and provided the Buddha with food and drink of a hundred flavors.
The Buddha said to Yaya:
"You should believe that practicing generosity always yields merit; in a future life, you shall be reborn into the family of this elder."
Yuye replied, "Yes.
When the Buddha had finished his meal, he gave a blessing and recited verses of aspiration:
"Fifty benevolent deities shall protect your person.
The Buddha told Yuye:
"Diligently recollect the sutras and the precepts."
Yujie said, "I have received the Buddha's grace in being permitted to hear the sutras and the Dharma.
They all stepped forward to pay homage to the Buddha and then withdrew.
The Sūtra of the Noble Lady (Ratnāvalī)
